SWIFT: Self-guided Weak-to-strong dIFfusion models via Target extrapolation

Yanjin He1,2,♯, Cuifeng Shen2, Wanzhou Lei2,3,♯, Maohua Li2,4,♯ Tao Lan2, Kan Liu2, Hanlin Tang†,2, Qing Qu1 Affiliation: 1University of Michigan, Ann Arbor  2Alibaba Group
3University of California, Berkeley  4Nanjing University
Abstract

Training high-quality diffusion models is computationally expensive, and inference-time guidance often adds further sampling cost. In this work, we introduce Swift, a simple yet effective self-guided training method that uses a frozen weak denoiser to improve a stronger model without adding inference overhead. For each noisy input, Swift extrapolates the clean regression target away from the weak denoiser’s prediction, amplifying components that remain underfit. The weak guide can be an early training checkpoint, requires no backpropagation during main-model training, and is discarded afterward. The resulting model retains the original sampler and supports both conditional and unconditional generation without label dropout or an unconditional branch. We explain this mechanism through a spectral analysis of finite-time population gradient flow in an RKHS. With an early-stopped weak guide, we prove that a nonempty range of extrapolation strengths yields strictly lower posterior-mean error than matched standard training, despite shifting the regression target away from the posterior mean. Experiments on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-256 demonstrate improvements across model scales and representations. In one ImageNet-256 configuration, Swift surpasses the baseline’s best FID using roughly half the total training compute, including guide preparation and training overhead. On RAEv2, it achieves FID 1.151.15 without inference-time guidance and 0.99 with guidance. These results establish target extrapolation as an effective approach to weak-to-strong diffusion training with efficient single-model inference.

††footnotetext: †\daggerProject lead  ♯Work done during internship at Alibaba

1 Introduction

Diffusion models have achieved strong generative performance across images, video, and audio [8, 9, 12]. They are typically trained with a simple denoising regression objective, yet many of the strongest generation results rely on guidance applied only at inference [7, 11]. In particular, autoguidance [11] shows that a deliberately weaker denoiser can improve a stronger one by defining an extrapolation direction during sampling. This suggests a broader role for weak models: rather than serving as teachers to imitate, they can provide directions along which a stronger predictor should move.

Autoguidance realizes this idea by extrapolating the strong model’s prediction away from that of a smaller or less-trained counterpart [11]. Related training-time approaches instead use evolving model predictions, intermediate supervision, or guidance-conditioned objectives [28, 39, 2, 36] (Section 8). These developments motivate a simple question:

We introduce Swift, a self-guided training method that uses a frozen weak denoiser to construct extrapolated regression targets. For each noisy input, instead of regressing directly toward the clean sample, Swift moves the target farther in the direction from the weak prediction toward and beyond the clean sample. The weak denoiser therefore acts as a directional reference, rather than a teacher whose output should be imitated. It can be obtained from an early checkpoint of ordinary denoising training, remains fixed during the main training run, and requires no backpropagation. After training, the guide is discarded, leaving a single denoiser and the original sampling procedure. The same construction applies to both conditional and unconditional generation.

Our motivation is finite-time underfitting: because a weak denoiser has learned less of the target function, extrapolating away from its prediction can amplify directions that remain underfit. We show theoretically that, for a nonempty range of positive extrapolation strengths, deliberately shifting the training target in this way can produce a predictor strictly closer to the original posterior mean than matched standard training (Theorem 4.1; proof in Section 7.4).

Experiments on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-256 show that the effect is not tied to a particular representation or model family. On ImageNet-256, Swift improves diffusion models built on conventional VAE latents, representation-autoencoder latents [38, 26], end-to-end learned latent representations, and direct pixel-space generation. Across the evaluated DiffusionBench configurations [16], the same fixed Swift recipe lowers unguided FID in every configuration, and the improvement persists under longer training. The complete ImageNet comparisons and training trajectories are in Sections 11.1 and 11.4, and the additional CIFAR-10 experiments are in Section 12.

Swift also remains complementary to inference-time guidance. When guidance is independently retuned for the baseline and Swift, the Swift model achieves lower FID in every tested configuration (Tables 7 and 10.2). Moreover, on RAEv2 the preferred internal-guidance scale decreases from 1.781.78 for the baseline to 1.201.20 after Swift training, while the best guided gFID improves from 1.041.04 to 0.990.99 (Figure 4(b); Section 11.3). This is consistent with Swift internalizing part of the weak-to-strong correction during training while leaving additional room for inference-time guidance.

Our contributions are:

  • •

    Weak-to-strong learning through target extrapolation. We introduce Swift, which uses a frozen weak denoiser as a directional reference to extrapolate clean-sample regression targets. The guide is fixed during main-model training and discarded at inference (Section 2.2).

  • •

    Broad improvements across diffusion representations. We demonstrate consistent gains across CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-256, spanning VAE, RAE, end-to-end latent, and pixel-space diffusion models. The gains persist under longer training and remain after inference-time guidance is independently retuned (Sections 5.1 and 5.2).

  • •

    A finite-training explanation. We show theoretically that target extrapolation can strictly reduce posterior-mean error relative to matched standard training over a nonempty range of positive extrapolation strengths (Section 4).

2 Swift: Self-Guided Training of Diffusion Models

2.1 Preliminaries

Denoising diffusion models generate samples by reversing Gaussian corruption [8, 10]. Let t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1] index the noise level, not the training iteration, and let σt\sigma_{t} increase with tt. We use the additive-noise parameterization

𝒙t=𝒙0+𝜺t,𝒙0∼pdata,𝜺t∼𝒩⁡(𝟎,σt2​𝐈d).\bm{x}_{t}=\bm{x}_{0}+\bm{\varepsilon}_{t},\qquad\bm{x}_{0}\sim p_{\mathrm{data}},\qquad\bm{\varepsilon}_{t}\sim\mathcal{N}(\bm{0},\sigma_{t}^{2}\mathbf{I}_{d}).

The noise 𝜺t\bm{\varepsilon}_{t} is independent of 𝒙0\bm{x}_{0}. We write ptp_{t} for the distribution of 𝒙t\bm{x}_{t} at fixed tt. When a condition 𝒄\bm{c} is present, it is an additional denoiser input; we suppress it below and discuss conditional and null-condition predictions in Section 3.

Training.

Standard clean-sample prediction [29, 10] trains a denoiser 𝒟𝜽​(𝒙t,σt)\mathcal{D}_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{x}_{t},\sigma_{t}) to predict 𝒙0\bm{x}_{0} by minimizing

ℒbase​(𝜽)=𝔼⁡[λ⁡(t)​‖𝒟𝜽​(𝒙t,σt)−𝒙0‖22],\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{base}}(\bm{\theta})=\mathbb{E}\left[\lambda(t)\left\|\mathcal{D}_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{x}_{t},\sigma_{t})-\bm{x}_{0}\right\|_{2}^{2}\right], (1)

where t∼pnoiset\sim p_{\mathrm{noise}} is sampled independently of 𝒙0∼pdata\bm{x}_{0}\sim p_{\mathrm{data}}, and pnoisep_{\mathrm{noise}} is the distribution of noise levels used during training. The expectation also includes 𝜺t\bm{\varepsilon}_{t} drawn as above, and λ⁡(t)>0\lambda(t)>0 on the support of pnoisep_{\mathrm{noise}}. With finite second moments, the unrestricted population minimizer of Eq. 1 is the posterior mean 𝒟⋆(𝒙t,σt)=𝔼[𝒙0∣𝒙t,t]\mathcal{D}^{\star}(\bm{x}_{t},\sigma_{t})=\mathbb{E}[\bm{x}_{0}\mid\bm{x}_{t},t] (Section 7.1). For σt>0\sigma_{t}>0, Tweedie’s formula relates it to the score [4]:

∇𝒙t​log​pt​(𝒙t)=𝒟⋆​(𝒙t,σt)−𝒙tσt2.\nabla_{\bm{x}_{t}}\log p_{t}(\bm{x}_{t})=\frac{\mathcal{D}^{\star}(\bm{x}_{t},\sigma_{t})-\bm{x}_{t}}{\sigma_{t}^{2}}. (2)

Inference.

With a differentiable variance-exploding noise schedule, the probability-flow ODE is [27]

d​𝒙t=−σ˙t​σt​∇𝒙t​log⁡pt​(𝒙t)​d​t.d\bm{x}_{t}=-\dot{\sigma}_{t}\sigma_{t}\nabla_{\bm{x}_{t}}\log p_{t}(\bm{x}_{t})\,dt. (3)

Sampling starts at a large noise level, where the noisy marginal can be approximated by a Gaussian, and integrates Eq. 3 toward smaller tt. In practice, the score in Eq. 2 is formed using the trained denoiser 𝒟𝜽\mathcal{D}_{\bm{\theta}} in place of 𝒟⋆\mathcal{D}^{\star}. Thus the sampler depends on the denoiser reached after finite training.

2.2 Proposed Method: Learning with a Frozen Weak Guide

Building on the preliminaries, we introduce Swift, which trains a denoiser using extrapolated regression targets. Instead of regressing directly onto the clean sample 𝒙0\bm{x}_{0} as in Eq. 1, Swift minimizes

ℒSWIFT​(𝜽)=𝔼⁡[λ⁡(t)​‖𝒟𝜽​(𝒙t,σt)−𝒚α‖22],\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SWIFT}}(\bm{\theta})=\mathbb{E}\left[\lambda(t)\left\|\mathcal{D}_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{x}_{t},\sigma_{t})-{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\bm{y}_{\alpha}}\right\|_{2}^{2}\right], (4)

with the same expectation and weighting as in Eq. 1, but using the extrapolated target:

\tcboxmath​[c​o​l​b​a​c​k=w​h​i​t​e,o​p​a​c​i​t​y​b​a​c​k=1,c​o​l​f​r​a​m​e=b​l​a​c​k!​75!​w​h​i​t​e,b​o​x​r​u​l​e=1.6​p​t,a​r​c=5​p​t,b​o​x​s​e​p=0​p​t,l​e​f​t=12​p​t,r​i​g​h​t=12​p​t,t​o​p=8​p​t,b​o​t​t​o​m=8​p​t]​𝒚α=𝒙0+α⁡(𝒙0−𝒟weak​(𝒙t,σt))\tcboxmath[colback=white,opacityback=1,colframe=black!75!white,boxrule=1.6pt,arc=5pt,boxsep=0pt,left=12pt,right=12pt,top=8pt,bottom=8pt]{{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\bm{y}_{\alpha}}=\bm{x}_{0}+\alpha\bigl(\bm{x}_{0}-\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{weak}}(\bm{x}_{t},\sigma_{t})\bigr)} (5)

Here, 𝒟weak\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{weak}} is a pretrained, frozen weak denoiser, and α≥0\alpha\geq 0 sets the extrapolation strength. Setting α=0\alpha=0 recovers standard denoising training. For α>0\alpha>0, the target extends beyond the clean sample in the direction away from the weak denoiser’s prediction. Velocity-predicting models [18] apply the same extrapolation to the velocity, which is equivalent (Section 10.1).

Constructing the frozen weak denoiser.

We train 𝒟weak\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{weak}} in the ordinary way with Eq. 1 and freeze it before the main run. The default guide uses a smaller architecture; capacity and training-stage variants are studied separately. The default DiffusionBench guide has approximately one quarter as many parameters as the main denoiser and is trained for half the main model’s standard training duration; the CIFAR-10 and RAEv2 guide checkpoints are specified in Section 10.1. The method is self-guided because the correction comes from a weaker denoiser trained on the same task, without an external teacher, a separate guidance objective, or an auxiliary prediction head.

The intuition is to compensate for what ordinary training has not learned within a finite training budget. Extrapolating the clean target away from 𝒟weak\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{weak}} emphasizes directions in which the weak denoiser’s prediction remains inaccurate. Whether this improves the main denoiser’s approximation to the posterior mean depends on how those directions relate to its own finite-training error. For a frozen weak denoiser obtained by early stopping ordinary training, Sections 4 and 4.1 establish conditions under which Swift achieves strictly lower posterior-mean error than baseline training (proofs in Section 7; a Gaussian-mixture illustration is in Section 9).

Training and inference.

During training, only the main denoiser 𝒟𝜽\mathcal{D}_{\bm{\theta}} is optimized with Eq. 4. The weak denoiser 𝒟weak\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{weak}} is evaluated without gradients and remains fixed. Thus, for a fixed clean sample, noise realization, and noise level, the regression target does not change as the main denoiser is updated. Beyond preparing the weak denoiser, each training step requires one additional weak-denoiser forward pass (about 9%9\% more FLOPs on DiffusionBench; Section 10.3). After training, it is discarded; sampling uses the trained denoiser and the original sampler, with no additional inference-time model evaluation (Section 10.2).

3 From Autoguidance to Self-Guided Training

A visual comparison.

Following the fractal-like Gaussian-mixture example of Karras et al. [11], we compare how different methods reproduce a distribution with thin, branching support. In Figure 2, Swift has the lowest reported KL divergence and outlier rate and the highest reported log⁡p\log p among the seven methods. Relative to GFT, the strongest baseline on these three reported metrics, its KL decreases from 0.8170.817 to 0.7280.728, its outlier rate from 4.97%4.97\% to 3.66%3.66\%, and its log⁡p\log p increases from −0.40-0.40 to +0.08+0.08. The highlighted regions show how the generated samples follow the narrow branches.

Inference-time guidance includes classifier-free guidance (CFG) [7] and autoguidance (AG) [11]. Training-based approaches include Model Guidance (MG) [28], Segmented Guidance (SGG) [36], and Guidance-Free Training (GFT) [2]. Internal Guidance (IG) [39] trains an intermediate output for guidance at sampling time. Additional comparisons appear in Sections 8 and 2.

3.1 From Sampling-Time Guidance to Training Targets

CFG combines conditional and unconditional predictions during sampling. AG is closer to Swift in its use of a weak denoiser. Let 𝒟base\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{base}} be a denoiser trained with the standard objective in Eq. 1. At the same noisy input and noise level, AG evaluates

𝒟AG=(1+α)​𝒟base−α​𝒟weak\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{AG}}=(1+\alpha)\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{base}}-\alpha\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{weak}}

during sampling. This requires the weak prediction whenever AG is applied. In Eq. 5, Swift instead places the observed clean sample 𝒙0\bm{x}_{0} in the position occupied by 𝒟base\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{base}} and uses the extrapolation as a training target. The weak denoiser is discarded after training.

Conditioned on (𝒙t,t)(\bm{x}_{t},t), the expectation of the Swift target is

(1+α)​𝒟⋆​(𝒙t,σt)−α​𝒟weak​(𝒙t,σt),(1+\alpha)\mathcal{D}^{\star}(\bm{x}_{t},\sigma_{t})-\alpha\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{weak}}(\bm{x}_{t},\sigma_{t}),

the expression obtained by applying AG to the ideal posterior mean (Lemma A.1). AG extrapolates a baseline denoiser already trained for a finite time, while Swift changes the regression target before main-model training. Under the assumptions of Section 4, this change can improve approximation to the original posterior mean; it is not a guarantee for every weak denoiser.

3.2 Comparison with Training-Based Guidance

MG constructs a training correction using conditional and unconditional model predictions [28]. SGG studies incorporating guidance into training using an updated weak network or an intermediate prediction branch in its training-time variants [36]. GFT trains across guidance strengths using an unconditional prediction [2]. In these constructions, the auxiliary predictions can change as their models are trained. IG jointly supervises intermediate and final outputs for sampling-time guidance; it also studies training with a detached final-minus-intermediate EMA correction [39, Sec. 6].

These designs use a changing prediction in the training correction or supervise an additional output. Swift obtains 𝒟weak\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{weak}} by ordinary denoising training and freezes it before training the main denoiser. For a fixed training example and noise realization, its extrapolated target does not change as the main model is updated. This avoids joint optimization of the weak and main denoisers, which provided no clear additional endpoint benefit in our CIFAR-10 comparisons (Section 12), and leaves a single denoiser at inference. Preparing and evaluating the weak denoiser still incur training compute, which our compute comparisons account for (Section 10.3). Further methodological details appear in Sections 8, B.2 and B.3.

4 Why Swift Can Help

We compare ordinary denoising and Swift after the same finite main-model training time. The analysis uses population gradient flow at one fixed noise level.

Assumption 1 (Population data and matched kernel training).

Fix a noise level tt and a noisy–clean pair (𝒙0,𝒙t)(\bm{x}_{0},\bm{x}_{t}) with 𝔼​‖𝒙0‖22<∞\mathbb{E}\|\bm{x}_{0}\|_{2}^{2}<\infty. All runs use population expectations under the same joint law. The diffusion case has 𝒙t=𝒙0+𝜺\bm{x}_{t}=\bm{x}_{0}+\bm{\varepsilon}, with independent 𝜺∼𝒩⁡(𝟎,σt2​𝐈d)\bm{\varepsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(\bm{0},\sigma_{t}^{2}\mathbf{I}_{d}) and σt>0\sigma_{t}>0; the theorem only requires the joint law and moment condition above.

Fix a bounded, measurable, symmetric positive-semidefinite scalar kernel 𝖪\mathsf{K}. Every predictor starts from zero and follows population gradient flow for normalized squared loss in the same coordinate-wise RKHS ℋ𝖪d\mathcal{H}_{\mathsf{K}}^{d}. Choose 0≤Tg<T<∞0\leq T_{g}<T<\infty. An ordinary run on the clean label 𝒙0\bm{x}_{0} yields the guide at time TgT_{g}; freeze it and continue the ordinary trajectory to TT for the baseline. Train a separate Swift predictor from zero to the same time TT, using the label (1+α)​𝒙0−α​𝒟weak​(𝒙t)(1+\alpha)\bm{x}_{0}-\alpha\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{weak}}(\bm{x}_{t}) while the guide stays frozen. The two main runs thus share the data law, kernel, initialization, and optimization horizon.

Write P𝒙tP_{\bm{x}_{t}} for the noisy-input distribution and 𝒟⋆​(𝒙)=𝔼⁡[𝒙0∣𝒙t=𝒙]\mathcal{D}^{\star}(\bm{x})=\mathbb{E}[\bm{x}_{0}\mid\bm{x}_{t}=\bm{x}] for the posterior mean. Prediction error is measured in ℋ2=L2​(P𝒙t,ℝd)\mathcal{H}_{2}=L^{2}(P_{\bm{x}_{t}};\mathbb{R}^{d}). The kernel couples predictions at different noisy inputs; a finite-feature linear predictor is one example.

Objectives and training dynamics.

At the fixed noise level, ordinary training and Swift minimize

𝒥0​(𝒅)\displaystyle\mathcal{J}_{0}(\bm{d}) =12​𝔼​‖𝒅⁡(𝒙t)−𝒙0‖22,\displaystyle=\tfrac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}\|\bm{d}(\bm{x}_{t})-\bm{x}_{0}\|_{2}^{2}, (6)

For either loss, let 𝒚\bm{y} denote its regression label. Population gradient flow in the RKHS is

d​𝒅sd​s=−∇ℋ𝖪d12​𝔼​‖𝒅s​(𝒙t)−𝒚‖22,𝒅0=𝟎.\frac{d\bm{d}_{s}}{ds}=-\nabla_{\mathcal{H}_{\mathsf{K}}^{d}}\tfrac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}\|\bm{d}_{s}(\bm{x}_{t})-\bm{y}\|_{2}^{2},\qquad\bm{d}_{0}=\bm{0}. (7)

∇𝒥​(𝒅)​(𝒙)=𝔼⁡[𝖪⁡(𝒙,𝒙t)​(𝒅⁡(𝒙t)−𝒚)].\nabla\mathcal{J}(\bm{d})(\bm{x})=\mathbb{E}[\mathsf{K}(\bm{x},\bm{x}_{t})(\bm{d}(\bm{x}_{t})-\bm{y})]. (8)

The resulting predictors are denoted by 𝒟weak\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{weak}}, 𝒟base\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{base}}, and 𝒟SWIFT(α)\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{SWIFT}}^{(\alpha)}, respectively. The guide is weaker here through shorter training in the same RKHS; Corollary A.12 also treats a spectrally nested smaller guide.

Finite-time response.

For any label 𝒚\bm{y}, let 𝒈⁡(𝒙)=𝔼⁡[𝒚∣𝒙t=𝒙]\bm{g}(\bm{x})=\mathbb{E}[\bm{y}\mid\bm{x}_{t}=\bm{x}]. The two conditional-mean targets are 𝒈0=𝒟⋆\bm{g}_{0}=\mathcal{D}^{\star} and

𝒈α=𝒟⋆+α⁡(𝒟⋆−𝒟weak).\bm{g}_{\alpha}=\mathcal{D}^{\star}+\alpha(\mathcal{D}^{\star}-\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{weak}}). (9)

The latter identity and its denoising-MSE interpretation are proved in Lemma A.1. Define the population kernel operator on ℋ2\mathcal{H}_{2} by

(𝓛​𝒇)​(𝒙)=∫𝖪⁡(𝒙,𝒙′)​𝒇​(𝒙′)​d​P𝒙t​(𝒙′).(\bm{\mathcal{L}}\bm{f})(\bm{x})=\int\mathsf{K}(\bm{x},\bm{x}^{\prime})\bm{f}(\bm{x}^{\prime})\,dP_{\bm{x}_{t}}(\bm{x}^{\prime}). (10)

It is bounded, self-adjoint, and positive semidefinite. Kernel gradient flow yields

d​𝒅sd​s=−𝓛⁡(𝒅s−𝒈),𝒅s=𝐇s​𝒈,𝐇s:=𝐈−e−s​𝓛.\frac{d\bm{d}_{s}}{ds}=-\bm{\mathcal{L}}(\bm{d}_{s}-\bm{g}),\qquad\bm{d}_{s}=\mathbf{H}_{s}\bm{g},\quad\mathbf{H}_{s}:=\mathbf{I}-e^{-s\bm{\mathcal{L}}}. (11)

The response 𝐇s\mathbf{H}_{s} learns a fraction 1−e−s​κ1-e^{-s\kappa} of a kernel mode with eigenvalue κ>0\kappa>0. The operator construction and solution of the flow appear in Section 7.2.

Theorem 4.1 (Finite-time improvement from a frozen weak denoiser).

Under Assumption 1,

𝒟weak\displaystyle\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{weak}} =𝐇Tg​𝒟⋆,\displaystyle=\mathbf{H}_{T_{g}}\mathcal{D}^{\star}, 𝒟base\displaystyle\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{base}} =𝐇T​𝒟⋆,\displaystyle=\mathbf{H}_{T}\mathcal{D}^{\star},
𝒟SWIFT(α)\displaystyle\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{SWIFT}}^{(\alpha)} =𝐇T​[(1+α)​𝒟⋆−α​𝒟weak].\displaystyle=\mathbf{H}_{T}[(1+\alpha)\mathcal{D}^{\star}-\alpha\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{weak}}].

If 𝐇T​𝒟⋆≠𝟎\mathbf{H}_{T}\mathcal{D}^{\star}\neq\bm{0}, the guide has strictly larger posterior-mean risk than the baseline. Moreover, for R⁡(α)=‖𝒟SWIFT(α)−𝒟⋆‖ℋ22R(\alpha)=\|\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{SWIFT}}^{(\alpha)}-\mathcal{D}^{\star}\|_{\mathcal{H}_{2}}^{2}, there is an α⋆>0\alpha^{\star}>0 such that

R⁡(α)<R⁡(0)(0<α<α⋆).R(\alpha)<R(0)\qquad(0<\alpha<\alpha^{\star}). (12)

Section 7.4 proves both claims using Theorem A.5. An earlier guide has learned less of each learnable mode; a small positive extrapolation partially cancels the baseline’s finite-time residual. The modewise calculation is Eq. A.10, and a larger coefficient can overshoot. The result concerns population denoising MSE at equal main-model optimization time, with guide preparation excluded; it does not directly imply a FID improvement. A Gaussian-mixture example gives an explicit posterior mean (Lemma A.8), and for an RBF kernel Proposition A.10 verifies the nonzero-predictor condition. Sections 7.7 and 7.8 give complementary finite-step and finite-sample analyses.

5 Experiments

We evaluate Swift on ImageNet-256 [3] and CIFAR-10 [13]. In every experiment Swift changes only the regression target; architectures, training schedules, samplers, and evaluation pipelines are kept the same as the baseline. On ImageNet, Swift uses one fixed recipe unless stated otherwise: α=0.4\alpha{=}0.4 with a smaller pretrained guide frozen before main-model training. The default DiffusionBench guide is trained for half the main model’s standard training duration (Section 10.1).

Evaluation setup.

Inspired by DiffusionBench [16], we evaluate Swift across 19 ImageNet-256 model configurations. For each configuration, we compare the baseline and Swift with and without inference-time guidance, tuning both guidance strengths separately where checkpoints are available and identifying published baselines otherwise. We report FID [6], sFID [21], precision and recall [14], representation-space FDr [32], and MIND [1] where available. Table 1 shows selected results; training and evaluation settings are in Sections 10.1 and 10.2, with complete ImageNet-256 and CIFAR-10 results in Sections 11 and 12.

5.1 Generation Quality and Transfer Across Representations

Matched improvements.

Table 1 isolates the target change within each model configuration. On RAE/DINOv2-B features [30, 38, 22], Swift lowers unguided FID from 2.092.09 to 1.751.75 and the five-feature mean FDr from 4.134.13 to 3.693.69 after 80 epochs. The gain persists on the independent RAEv2/DINOv3-L configuration [26], where unguided FID improves from 1.561.56 to 1.151.15 within a 160-epoch training budget; the Swift value is selected at epoch 140 (Section 10.2).

Transfer with one fixed recipe.

Across 18 DiffusionBench configurations spanning latent and pixel representations, one fixed recipe lowers unguided FID in every case, by 16.3%16.3\%–49.4%49.4\% (median 31.3%31.3\%). Even the three lowest-FID baselines improve by 16.3%16.3\%–17.4%17.4\%. FDr and MIND each improve in at least 17 of 18 configurations in every feature space. Full results appear in Table 6.

Compatibility with inference guidance.

At the best available guidance settings, Swift also lowers guided FID in all 18 DiffusionBench configurations (Table 7). On RAEv2, Swift improves internal-guidance FID from 1.041.04 to 0.990.99 (Table 1), while its unguided FID improves from 1.561.56 to 1.151.15. Representative samples from the 0.990.99-gFID model are shown in Figure 3; additional class-conditional samples appear in Section 13.

5.2 Combining Swift with Inference-Time Guidance

We combine Swift with autoguidance [11] on the DiffusionBench models and native internal REPA-head guidance on RAEv2 [26]. These mechanisms apply a weak-to-strong extrapolation at sampling time, whereas Swift learns a related correction during training and then discards its guide. We ask whether inference-time guidance still improves a Swift-trained model and whether Swift changes the preferred guidance strength.

Across all five configurations in Figure 4(a), the same ordering appears. Swift improves the unguided baseline, inference-time guidance improves it further, and independently retuned guidance on top of Swift gives the best FID in every case. This shows that the improvement learned during training is not replaced by inference-time guidance: even after the baseline has been separately retuned for guidance, the Swift model retains an additional gain.

Swift also changes the preferred inference-time guidance strength. On RAEv2, the optimal internal-guidance scale shifts from 1.781.78 for the baseline to 1.201.20 for Swift, while the best guided FID improves from 1.041.04 to 0.990.99 (Figure 4(b); Section 11.3). The lower preferred scale is consistent with overlap between the training-time and inference-time corrections. The remaining gain shows that inference-time guidance remains complementary to the correction learned during training.

5.3 Longer Training and Training Cost

The gain persists with longer training.

We continue the matched DINOv2-B pair to 240 epochs. Swift is ahead at all 36 evaluations from epochs 20 to 240, with the gap growing from 0.120.12 to 0.260.26 FID, with the training-time evaluator giving →1.381.63\!\to\!1.38 at epoch 240. A separate baseline continued to 320 epochs reaches at best 1.531.53, still above the 1.501.50 reached by Swift at epoch 120. The matched training-time FIDs are listed in Table 9 and plotted in Figure 10; four additional trajectories appear in Figures 9 and 11.4.

Training cost.

Swift adds 9%9\% FLOPs per epoch for the frozen guide, plus roughly 10 baseline-equivalent epochs to pretrain it (Section 10.3). For context, MG and SGG incur about 1.23×1.23\times and 1.22×1.22\times wall-clock time per training iteration in the unified SiT-B/2 comparison of Yuan et al. [36, Table 6], while GFT reports 10–20% additional computation per training update [2]. IG reports negligible extra sampling FLOPs [39, App. B]. Charging both of our costs, Swift at epoch 120 already surpasses the best DINOv2-B baseline result observed through 320 epochs (1.531.53), using approximately 0.45×0.45\times the FLOPs needed to reach that baseline checkpoint (Figure 5). On RAEv2, epoch-50 Swift similarly improves on the epoch-160 baseline (1.341.34 vs. 1.561.56) at 0.44×0.44\times the FLOPs (including guide preparation; Section 10.3).

These time-to-quality ratios are conservative: within the observed training horizon, the baselines never reach the best Swift FID. No baseline time-to-quality is observed for those targets.

5.4 How to Choose α\alpha and the Weak Guide

Choosing α\alpha.

Performance is broadly U-shaped in α\alpha (Figure 6(a)). On CIFAR-10, moderate positive values form a broad favorable region around α=0.7\alpha=0.7–0.90.9, where differences are comparable to replicate noise. ImageNet shows the same qualitative behavior: on DINOv2-B, α∈[0.5,1.0]\alpha\in[0.5,1.0] substantially improves over the baseline. The precise optimum depends on the model, however, so our breadth experiments use the fixed default α=0.4\alpha=0.4 without tuning; in practice, a small sweep over moderate positive values is sufficient. Negative α\alpha can accelerate the initial decrease in FID, but the tested negative warm starts provide no consistent final-quality advantage (Section 12).

Choosing the weak guide.

The guide should be weaker than the student, but still competent. At α=0.8\alpha=0.8 on CIFAR-10, reducing the channel base from the student’s 128 to 64 improves FID from 2.582.58 to 1.601.60, while substantially smaller guides degrade rapidly (Figure 6(b)). The half-width guide is also the best width across the tested α\alpha values on CIFAR-10 and consistently outperforms wider alternatives on ImageNet. Guide training length shows a similar pattern: once the guide crosses a competence threshold, performance is relatively insensitive over a broad range (Figure 6(c)). On ImageNet, freezing the guide earlier can even help, with an earlier guide outperforming the default guide in our 50k re-evaluation; the corresponding training trajectories are discussed in Section 11.4.

A simple fixed recipe gives substantial gains.

The full CIFAR-10 campaign also tests jointly trained guides, capacity switches, and coefficients that change with training time or noise level (Sections 12 and 10). Co-training provides no clear additional endpoint benefit in the tested comparisons. Some early capacity switches and late coefficient profiles give useful CIFAR-10 refinements, whereas other schedules lose the gain; their effects depend on the guide and coefficient, and many small differences remain unresolved by repetitions. We therefore retain a frozen half-width guide and a fixed, moderate positive α\alpha as the simple default for the broader experiments.

6 Conclusion

The regression target has received comparatively little attention as a design choice in diffusion training, yet it turns out to be a simple and effective place to intervene. By carrying the clean target past itself and away from a frozen weak model, Swift moves a weak-to-strong correction from inference into training, leaving a single denoiser and the original sampler at deployment with only about 9%9\% additional main-training FLOPs. Crucially, the modified target is not itself a better estimator of the posterior mean: it is deliberately biased, yet finite training on it can produce a better final predictor and better samples. This suggests a broader view of the regression target as a design interface rather than a fixed quantity—and raises the question of what other useful corrections can be written into it.

Reproducibility statement

Swift changes only the regression target: the objective is Eqs. 4 and 5, the frozen weak denoiser is constructed as described in Section 2.2, and everything else is the training loop of the respective framework. Section 10.1 specifies guide architectures, freezing points, coefficients, training budgets, and hardware for the EDM, DiffusionBench, and RAEv2 models, and explains the velocity-target implementation. Section 10.2 specifies samplers, guidance and checkpoint selection, and evaluation metrics, distinguishing re-evaluated pairs from published baselines; Section 10.3 reports the GPU hours and the FLOPs accounting behind Figures 1 and 5. Section 11 gives all 19 ImageNet-256 configurations with and without guidance on all 15 metrics, and Section 12 the CIFAR-10 experiments, including an account of all 156 launched (152 scored) arms (Section 12). The matched Gaussian-mixture comparison is specified in Section 9, and all assumptions and proofs are in Section 7. Our implementation will be made publicly available upon publication.

AI use statement

We used large language models (LLMs) in preparing this paper. They edited the text for clarity; drafted parts of the text, including appendix sections, from our experiment logs and notes; generated LaTeX and TikZ code for tables and figures; computed summary statistics from our result files. The authors reviewed and revised all LLM-assisted content and take full responsibility for the paper.

Thus posterior-mean risk and population clean-target MSE induce the same ordering of predictors. The target shift is beneficial only through the training response; it does not improve the unrestricted population optimum.

7.2 Kernel training response

The following lemma establishes the prediction-space equation and the operator properties needed for the spectral proof, without requiring finite-dimensional features or 𝒈\bm{g} to belong to the RKHS.

Lemma A.3 (Prediction-space kernel flow).

Let 𝐲\bm{y} be a square-integrable vector regression target with conditional mean 𝐠⁡(𝐱t)=𝔼⁡[𝐲∣𝐱t]\bm{g}(\bm{x}_{t})=\mathbb{E}[\bm{y}\mid\bm{x}_{t}]. dd​s​𝒅s=−𝓛⁡(𝒅s−𝒈),𝒅0=𝟎,\frac{d}{ds}\bm{d}_{s}=-\bm{\mathcal{L}}(\bm{d}_{s}-\bm{g}),\qquad\bm{d}_{0}=\bm{0}, (A.5)

and therefore

𝒅s=𝐇s​𝒈,𝐇s=𝐈−e−s​𝓛.\bm{d}_{s}=\mathbf{H}_{s}\bm{g},\qquad\mathbf{H}_{s}=\mathbf{I}-e^{-s\bm{\mathcal{L}}}.

The conditional variance of 𝐲\bm{y} affects the value of the loss but not this population trajectory.

For the weighted diffusion loss, the normalized time is s=2​λ​(t)​τs=2\lambda(t)\tau, where τ\tau is time under the unnormalized objective. It suffices to prove injectivity for one scalar coordinate. Let f∈L2​(P𝐱t)f\in L^{2}(P_{\bm{x}_{t}}) and suppose 𝓛0​f=0\bm{\mathcal{L}}_{0}f=0. Then ⟨f,𝓛0​f⟩L2​(P𝐱t)=0\langle f,\bm{\mathcal{L}}_{0}f\rangle_{L^{2}(P_{\bm{x}_{t}})}=0. The signed measure d​η​(𝐱t)=f⁡(𝐱t)​d​P𝐱t​(𝐱t)d\eta(\bm{x}_{t})=f(\bm{x}_{t})dP_{\bm{x}_{t}}(\bm{x}_{t}) has finite total variation by Cauchy–Schwarz. Use the convention η^​(𝛚)=∫e−i​𝛚⊤​𝐱​𝑑η​(𝐱)\widehat{\eta}(\bm{\omega})=\int e^{-i\bm{\omega}^{\top}\bm{x}}\,d\eta(\bm{x}). The Gaussian Fourier identity is

e−∥𝒛∥22/(2ℓ2)=cd,ℓ∫ℝdei​𝝎⊤​𝒛e−ℓ2∥𝝎∥22/2d𝝎,cd,ℓ=(ℓ2​π)d.e^{-\|\bm{z}\|_{2}^{2}/(2\ell^{2})}=c_{d,\ell}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}e^{i\bm{\omega}^{\top}\bm{z}}e^{-\ell^{2}\|\bm{\omega}\|_{2}^{2}/2}\,d\bm{\omega},\qquad c_{d,\ell}=\left(\frac{\ell}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\right)^{d}.

The Gaussian multiplier is integrable and η\eta has finite total variation, so Fubini’s theorem applies after integrating this identity against d​η​(𝐱)​d​η​(𝐱′)d\eta(\bm{x})\,d\eta(\bm{x}^{\prime}) with 𝐳=𝐱−𝐱′\bm{z}=\bm{x}-\bm{x}^{\prime}. It gives

⟨f,𝓛0f⟩=cd,ℓ∫ℝd|η^(𝝎)|2e−ℓ2∥𝝎∥22/2d𝝎,\langle f,\bm{\mathcal{L}}_{0}f\rangle=c_{d,\ell}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}|\widehat{\eta}(\bm{\omega})|^{2}e^{-\ell^{2}\|\bm{\omega}\|_{2}^{2}/2}\,d\bm{\omega},

The Gaussian Fourier multiplier is strictly positive everywhere, so zero energy implies that η^=0\widehat{\eta}=0 Lebesgue-almost everywhere. The Fourier transform of a finite signed measure is continuous, hence it vanishes everywhere; uniqueness of Fourier transforms of finite measures gives η=0\eta=0. Since d​η=f​d​P𝐱td\eta=f\,dP_{\bm{x}_{t}}, f=0f=0 P𝐱tP_{\bm{x}_{t}}-almost surely. Applying this coordinatewise proves injectivity.

Finally, the tower property and independence of the corruption noise give

𝔼⁡[𝒟⋆​(𝒙t)​𝒙t⊤]=𝔼⁡[𝒙0​𝒙t⊤]=𝔼⁡[𝒙0​𝒙0⊤]⪰𝚺≻𝟎.\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{D}^{\star}(\bm{x}_{t})\bm{x}_{t}^{\top}]=\mathbb{E}[\bm{x}_{0}\bm{x}_{t}^{\top}]=\mathbb{E}[\bm{x}_{0}\bm{x}_{0}^{\top}]\succeq\bm{\Sigma}\succ\mathbf{0}.

Thus 𝒟⋆\mathcal{D}^{\star} cannot vanish in ℋ2\mathcal{H}_{2}. Injectivity gives ker⁡𝓛={𝟎}\ker\bm{\mathcal{L}}=\{\bm{0}\}. For every T>0T>0, spectral calculus implies

ker⁡𝐇T=ker⁡(𝐈−e−T​𝓛)=ker⁡𝓛={𝟎}.\ker\mathbf{H}_{T}=\ker(\mathbf{I}-e^{-T\bm{\mathcal{L}}})=\ker\bm{\mathcal{L}}=\{\bm{0}\}.

Hence 𝒟base=𝐇T​𝒟⋆≠𝟎\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{base}}=\mathbf{H}_{T}\mathcal{D}^{\star}\neq\bm{0} in ℋ2\mathcal{H}_{2}, verifying the nonzero-predictor condition of Theorem 4.1.

The Gaussian kernel is injective, so every nonzero posterior mean has learnable signal. The theorem therefore does not require a deliberately underpowered function class.

7.6 Reduced-rank and spectrally nested guides

A narrower guide can be modeled by retaining a subset of the main model’s learning directions. The projection below specifies the spectral nesting needed for this interpretation.

Let 𝐏g\mathbf{P}_{g} be an orthogonal projection on ℋ2\mathcal{H}_{2} satisfying

𝐏g​𝓛=𝓛​𝐏g.\mathbf{P}_{g}\bm{\mathcal{L}}=\bm{\mathcal{L}}\mathbf{P}_{g}.

For example, 𝐏g\mathbf{P}_{g} may retain any subset of the eigenfunctions of 𝓛\bm{\mathcal{L}}; if it retains finitely many, the guide response is finite rank. For 0<T<∞0<T<\infty and 0≤Tg<∞0\leq T_{g}<\infty, define

𝐇c=𝐈−e−T​𝓛,𝐇g=𝐏g​(𝐈−e−Tg​𝓛).\mathbf{H}_{c}=\mathbf{I}-e^{-T\bm{\mathcal{L}}},\qquad\mathbf{H}_{g}=\mathbf{P}_{g}(\mathbf{I}-e^{-T_{g}\bm{\mathcal{L}}}). (A.17)
Corollary A.12 (Reduced-rank guide).

The operators in Eq. A.17 satisfy Eq. A.7. If 𝐇c​𝒟⋆≠𝟎\mathbf{H}_{c}\mathcal{D}^{\star}\neq\bm{0}, then A>0A>0 and C>0C>0 in Theorem A.5. Consequently, the Swift predictor has smaller posterior-mean risk than the baseline exactly for 0<α<2​A/C0<\alpha<2A/C.

Proof A.13.

Because 𝐏g\mathbf{P}_{g} is an orthogonal projection commuting with 𝓛\bm{\mathcal{L}}, 𝐇g\mathbf{H}_{g} is a positive self-adjoint contraction and commutes with 𝐇c\mathbf{H}_{c}. Moreover,

𝐈−𝐇g−e−Tg​𝓛=(𝐈−𝐏g)​(𝐈−e−Tg​𝓛)⪰𝟎.\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{H}_{g}-e^{-T_{g}\bm{\mathcal{L}}}=(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{P}_{g})(\mathbf{I}-e^{-T_{g}\bm{\mathcal{L}}})\succeq\mathbf{0}.

All factors commute, so the alignment obeys

A≥⟨𝒟⋆,e−(T+Tg)​𝓛​(𝐈−e−T​𝓛)​𝒟⋆⟩>0.A\geq\left\langle\mathcal{D}^{\star},e^{-(T+T_{g})\bm{\mathcal{L}}}(\mathbf{I}-e^{-T\bm{\mathcal{L}}})\mathcal{D}^{\star}\right\rangle>0.

The strict inequality follows because the multiplier e−(T+Tg)​κ​(1−e−T​κ)e^{-(T+T_{g})\kappa}(1-e^{-T\kappa}) is positive for every κ>0\kappa>0, and 𝐇c​𝒟⋆≠𝟎\mathbf{H}_{c}\mathcal{D}^{\star}\neq\bm{0} ensures a nonzero component in such a direction. Apply Theorem A.5.

This corollary is the rigorous counterpart of a reduced-width guide only when the narrower model corresponds to a nested spectral subspace. Arbitrary architectural width reduction need not preserve the eigenfunctions and is not covered without an additional approximation argument.

7.7 Exact label-affine response for finite-step training

We next separate a second exact statement from the population theorem. It applies to finite data and a finite number of optimization steps, provided the features are fixed. Let 𝒙t,1,…,𝒙t,n\bm{x}_{t,1},\ldots,\bm{x}_{t,n} be training inputs, let 𝚽∈ℝn×p\bm{\Phi}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times p} be a fixed design matrix, and train the vector-valued linear predictor 𝚽​𝚯\bm{\Phi}\bm{\Theta} with full-batch gradient descent:

𝚯s+1=𝚯s−γsn𝚽⊤(𝚽𝚯s−𝐘),s=0,…,S−1,\bm{\Theta}_{s+1}=\bm{\Theta}_{s}-\frac{\gamma_{s}}{n}\bm{\Phi}^{\top}(\bm{\Phi}\bm{\Theta}_{s}-\mathbf{Y}),\qquad s=0,\ldots,S-1,

where 𝐘∈ℝn×d\mathbf{Y}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d} is the label matrix. The initialization 𝚯0\bm{\Theta}_{0} and step sizes γs\gamma_{s} are fixed independently of the labels and held the same across target choices. No convergence assumption is made.

Proposition A.14 (Finite-step label affinity).

For every S≥0S\geq 0, there exist 𝐔S∈ℝp×d\mathbf{U}_{S}\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times d} and a linear operator 𝐀S:ℝn×d→ℝp×d\mathbf{A}_{S}:\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}\to\mathbb{R}^{p\times d}, both independent of 𝐘\mathbf{Y}, such that

𝚯S=𝐔S+𝐀S​(𝐘).\bm{\Theta}_{S}=\mathbf{U}_{S}+\mathbf{A}_{S}(\mathbf{Y}). (A.18)

Consequently, predictions under any fixed bounded linear evaluation map into a Hilbert prediction space are affine functions of the labels.

Proof A.15.

Set 𝐐s=𝐈p−γs​𝚽⊤​𝚽/n\mathbf{Q}_{s}=\mathbf{I}_{p}-\gamma_{s}\bm{\Phi}^{\top}\bm{\Phi}/n. Then

𝚯s+1=𝐐s​𝚯s+γsn​𝚽⊤​𝐘.\bm{\Theta}_{s+1}=\mathbf{Q}_{s}\bm{\Theta}_{s}+\frac{\gamma_{s}}{n}\bm{\Phi}^{\top}\mathbf{Y}.

The assertion holds at s=0s=0 with 𝐔0=𝚯0\mathbf{U}_{0}=\bm{\Theta}_{0} and 𝐀0=𝟎\mathbf{A}_{0}=\mathbf{0}. If it holds at step ss, it holds at step s+1s+1 with

𝐔s+1=𝐐s​𝐔s,𝐀s+1​(𝐘)=𝐐s​𝐀s​(𝐘)+γsn​𝚽⊤​𝐘.\mathbf{U}_{s+1}=\mathbf{Q}_{s}\mathbf{U}_{s},\qquad\mathbf{A}_{s+1}(\mathbf{Y})=\mathbf{Q}_{s}\mathbf{A}_{s}(\mathbf{Y})+\frac{\gamma_{s}}{n}\bm{\Phi}^{\top}\mathbf{Y}.

Induction proves Eq. A.18. Evaluation is linear in 𝚯S\bm{\Theta}_{S}, so it preserves affinity.

The same proof covers mini-batch schedules fixed in advance, fixed linear preconditioners, weight decay, and momentum after augmenting the state. It does not cover label-dependent feature learning without further assumptions. In particular, the fixed-feature response has the label-affine form assumed in Proposition A.16.

7.8 Finite-sample bias–variance extension

For finite data, target extrapolation also amplifies the conditional label noise. The resulting risk depends on both residual alignment and variance inflation. The following result is exact under conditional centering, which holds in the independent-data example below but is not automatic for a guide trained on the same clean labels.

Let ℱ\mathcal{F} be a sigma-algebra with respect to which the noisy training inputs, the response map, and the guide are measurable. It represents the information held fixed when averaging the remaining label randomness. Let 𝐌\mathbf{M} be the matrix of stacked posterior means and write the clean labels as

𝐌=(𝒟⋆​(𝒙t,1),…,𝒟⋆​(𝒙t,n))⊤∈ℝn×d,𝐗0=𝐌+𝐄,𝔼⁡[𝐄∣ℱ]=𝟎.\mathbf{M}=\bigl(\mathcal{D}^{\star}(\bm{x}_{t,1}),\ldots,\mathcal{D}^{\star}(\bm{x}_{t,n})\bigr)^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d},\qquad\mathbf{X}_{0}=\mathbf{M}+\mathbf{E},\qquad\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{E}\mid\mathcal{F}]=\mathbf{0}.

For example, the displayed conditional-centering assumption holds for i.i.d. training pairs when the guide is trained on an independent dataset and the response map and initialization depend only on the noisy inputs and independent algorithmic randomness, with ℱ\mathcal{F} generated by these noisy inputs, auxiliary data, and randomness. With 𝐘g\mathbf{Y}_{g} the stacked guide predictions and 𝚫g=𝐌−𝐘g\bm{\Delta}_{g}=\mathbf{M}-\mathbf{Y}_{g}, the Swift labels are

𝐘α=(1+α)​𝐗0−α​𝐘g=𝐌+α​𝚫g+(1+α)​𝐄.\mathbf{Y}_{\alpha}=(1+\alpha)\mathbf{X}_{0}-\alpha\mathbf{Y}_{g}=\mathbf{M}+\alpha\bm{\Delta}_{g}+(1+\alpha)\mathbf{E}.

Let the trained predictor in a Hilbert space 𝒴\mathcal{Y} have the exact label-affine form 𝒂+𝓖​𝐘\bm{a}+\bm{\mathcal{G}}\mathbf{Y}, where 𝒂\bm{a} and the bounded linear operator 𝓖\bm{\mathcal{G}} are ℱ\mathcal{F}-measurable, and 𝒴\mathcal{Y} is separable. Let 𝒅ev⋆∈𝒴\bm{d}^{\star}_{\mathrm{ev}}\in\mathcal{Y} be a fixed (or ℱ\mathcal{F}-measurable) posterior-mean target on the evaluation distribution. Assume 𝒂\bm{a}, 𝓖​𝐌\bm{\mathcal{G}}\mathbf{M}, 𝓖​𝚫g\bm{\mathcal{G}}\bm{\Delta}_{g}, 𝒅ev⋆\bm{d}^{\star}_{\mathrm{ev}}, and 𝓖​𝐄\bm{\mathcal{G}}\mathbf{E} are square-integrable 𝒴\mathcal{Y}-valued random variables, and set

𝒆\displaystyle\bm{e} =𝒅ev⋆−(𝒂+𝓖​𝐌),\displaystyle=\bm{d}^{\star}_{\mathrm{ev}}-(\bm{a}+\bm{\mathcal{G}}\mathbf{M}), 𝒒\displaystyle\bm{q} =𝓖​𝚫g,\displaystyle=\bm{\mathcal{G}}\bm{\Delta}_{g},
𝜼\displaystyle\bm{\eta} =𝓖​𝐄,\displaystyle=\bm{\mathcal{G}}\mathbf{E}, A\displaystyle A =⟨𝒆,𝒒⟩,\displaystyle=\langle\bm{e},\bm{q}\rangle,
C\displaystyle C =‖𝒒‖2,\displaystyle=\|\bm{q}\|^{2}, V\displaystyle V =𝔼⁡[‖𝜼‖2∣ℱ].\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[\|\bm{\eta}\|^{2}\mid\mathcal{F}].

These integrability assumptions make the conditional expectations well defined and ensure V<∞V<\infty almost surely. Then 𝔼⁡[𝜼∣ℱ]=𝟎\mathbb{E}[\bm{\eta}\mid\mathcal{F}]=\bm{0} and, exactly,

𝒅^α−𝒅ev⋆=−𝒆+α​𝒒+(1+α)​𝜼.\widehat{\bm{d}}_{\alpha}-\bm{d}^{\star}_{\mathrm{ev}}=-\bm{e}+\alpha\bm{q}+(1+\alpha)\bm{\eta}.
Proposition A.16 (Finite-sample variance tax).

Under the preceding conditional label-affine model, define

Rℱ​(α):=𝔼⁡[‖𝒅^α−𝒅ev⋆‖2∣ℱ].R_{\mathcal{F}}(\alpha):=\mathbb{E}[\|\widehat{\bm{d}}_{\alpha}-\bm{d}^{\star}_{\mathrm{ev}}\|^{2}\mid\mathcal{F}].

Then

𝔼⁡[‖𝒅^α−𝒅ev⋆‖2∣ℱ]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\|\widehat{\bm{d}}_{\alpha}-\bm{d}^{\star}_{\mathrm{ev}}\|^{2}\mid\mathcal{F}] =‖𝒆−α​𝒒‖2+(1+α)2​V,\displaystyle=\|\bm{e}-\alpha\bm{q}\|^{2}+(1+\alpha)^{2}V, (A.19)
Rℱ​(α)−Rℱ​(0)\displaystyle R_{\mathcal{F}}(\alpha)-R_{\mathcal{F}}(0) =−2​(A−V)​α
